title: Sandbox Options for CSM Skills Development Research Finding

tldr.content: No single sandbox is best for every CSM workload. Use a provider-neutral host broker with fail-closed policy: disposable copied workspaces, credential scrubbing, network denial, hard resource limits, and explicit cleanup. For local development, use rootless Docker now if its rootless mode is verified; use bubblewrap plus Landlock for lean Linux command paths; reserve gVisor, Kata, Firecracker, or Cloudflare Sandbox for hostile or high-value execution.

executiveSummary.content:
This DEEP hybrid investigation examined the CSM skill suite, existing sandbox policy, the current host, Linux isolation primitives, containers, gVisor, Kata, Firecracker, Cloudflare Sandbox, Claude Code sandboxing, and security guidance for model-generated code.

```text
CSM skill request
   -> trust/risk classification
   -> host-owned capability broker
      -> workspace/worktree copy
      -> sandbox provider
      -> network/credential/resource policy
      -> worker execution
   -> events, cleanup, artifact export, acceptance evidence
```

The local suite already distinguishes static analysis, trusted code, trusted-local snapshots, and hostile generated candidates. It also has explicit R0-R3 review guidance and fail-closed generated autoresearch contracts. The principal weakness is not the absence of policy; it is that enforcement is fragmented or delegated to an unavailable host provider. Temporary directories and Git worktrees are useful but are not security boundaries.

The recommended target is a layered execution broker. It should select a provider based on threat model and capability attestation, never silently downgrade. Worktree isolation handles concurrent code ownership; OS/container/VM isolation handles host blast radius; network and credential brokers handle exfiltration; cgroups and process-group cleanup handle denial of service; existing skill ledgers, cursors, receipts, and evidence gates remain authoritative.

keyFindings.content:
K1 [supported] Temporary directories provide disposal and collision hygiene, not hostile-code isolation. Git worktrees separate working files and indexes but share repository metadata and do not isolate processes, credentials, sockets, network, resources, or external state. [ref-git-worktree][ref-prior-sandbox]

K2 [supported] The CSM suite has materially different trust classes: static planning/DDD, disposable R&D, review R0-R3, execution-capable build/make-tests, and autoresearch registered/trusted-local/generated modes. Generated autoresearch requires a verified sandbox provider and fails closed when unavailable; trusted-local is explicitly not OS-isolated. [ref-plan-safety][ref-review-rungs][ref-autoresearch-contract][ref-autoresearch-runtime]

K3 [supported] Namespaces, `no_new_privs`, dropped capabilities, seccomp, Landlock, cgroups, and egress controls are defense-in-depth layers. Seccomp is explicitly not a complete sandbox; Landlock is stackable but limited; cgroups bound resources; strong egress policy must be enforced outside the untrusted process. [ref-seccomp][ref-landlock][ref-cgroups][ref-firecracker]

K4 [partially-supported] Bubblewrap is the best lean Linux command-launch primitive for this repository's small local paths because it is unprivileged, creates a controlled mount namespace, and composes user/PID/IPC/network/UTS/seccomp features. It is not universally best, has no native CPU/memory policy, and its own policy must be correct. [ref-bubblewrap]

K5 [supported] Landlock is best used as a complementary in-process filesystem/network restriction, not as a replacement for namespaces, identity controls, syscall policy, resource limits, or host egress. It is kernel-ABI-dependent and leaves deliberate coverage gaps. [ref-landlock]

K6 [partially-supported] NsJail is a strong single-wrapper alternative when explicit namespaces, seccomp, cgroups, filesystem, UID/GID, and resource policies are needed. Systemd is strong on host-integrated lifecycle/cgroups but less portable. Rootless Podman is attractive for daemonless OCI execution; rootless Docker is attractive where Docker ecosystem compatibility matters. These are operational preferences, not universal security rankings. [ref-nsjail][ref-systemd][ref-podman][ref-docker-rootless]

K7 [supported] Rootless Docker/Podman are useful for trusted or semi-trusted CSM jobs only when mounts, sockets, capabilities, credentials, cgroups, network, and cleanup are explicitly hardened. Ordinary containers share the host kernel and are not sufficient by themselves for high-value hostile code. [ref-docker-security][ref-podman][ref-gvisor]

K8 [supported with qualification] gVisor mediates syscalls through a user-space Sentry; Kata adds a guest kernel while retaining OCI compatibility; Firecracker provides a minimal KVM microVM plus Jailer and strong self-managed isolation; Cloudflare Sandbox provides a managed VM-backed isolated container option with quotas, lifecycle loss on stop, and outbound handlers. Each has compatibility, operational, cost, and provider-trust trade-offs. [ref-gvisor][ref-kata][ref-firecracker][ref-cloudflare-security][ref-cloudflare-lifecycle][ref-cloudflare-egress]

K9 [recommendation] For local CSM development, default to a host-controlled runner using a disposable copied workspace, verified rootless container or OS sandbox, scrubbed environment, network denial or an allowlisted proxy, hard resource/time/output limits, and fail-closed unavailable-provider behavior. Use stronger VM-backed providers for hostile generated code or high-value hosts. This is a proposed policy, not existing repository enforcement. [ref-claude-sandbox-environments][ref-local-sandbox-map]

K10 [partially-supported] csm-build is the highest-risk skill because it writes and executes repository code; csm-make-tests executes toolchains and generated tests; generated csm-autoresearch requires verified sandbox; csm-review already defines optional R0-R3; csm-plan and csm-ddd are predominantly read-only with bounded R&D or Git surfaces. Exact mandatory rung assignment remains a policy decision, not uniformly encoded in all contracts. [ref-local-sandbox-map]

K11 [recommendation] Add one host-owned execution/capability broker beneath csm-orchestrate. It should attest providers, canonicalize roots, scrub environment, enforce network/credential/resource policy, contain descendants, record redacted events, and export only explicit artifacts. Skills should declare requirements and consume this broker rather than implementing sandbox logic independently. [ref-local-seams][ref-local-sandbox-map]

K12 [supported] Sandbox-unavailable fallback must never silently become unsandboxed execution. Claude Code documents an explicit unsandboxed retry escape hatch and a strict setting; generated autoresearch already rejects missing or unverifiable sandbox capability. [ref-claude-sandboxing][ref-autoresearch-contract]

K13 [recommendation] Use a heuristic provider ladder: R0 no target execution; R1 temp/worktree; R2 rootless container or bubblewrap plus Landlock; R3 hardened container/gVisor/Kata; R4 Firecracker, dedicated VM, or managed remote sandbox. These labels describe policy strength, not standardized assurance, and every selected provider must attest actual controls. [ref-local-sandbox-map][ref-bubblewrap][ref-firecracker]

K14 [recommendation] Do not install Pi or another agent framework to solve this problem. First define provider-neutral sandbox contracts and integrate an available host-controlled provider behind an adapter; optional providers can be added after enforcement and failure-mode tests. [ref-local-sandbox-map][ref-prior-dynamic]

detailSections.content:
### Decision criteria

“Best” depends on the workload and threat model:

| Criterion | Question | Why it matters for CSM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Host isolation | Does untrusted code share the host kernel? | Determines breakout blast radius |
| Filesystem | Are reads/writes limited to a copied workspace? | Protects source, credentials, and CSM artifacts |
| Network | Is egress denied or mediated? | Limits exfiltration and supply-chain access |
| Identity | Does code run as the caller or a reduced identity? | Controls ambient privilege |
| Resources | Are CPU, memory, PIDs, disk, output, and time bounded? | Prevents denial of service and denial of wallet |
| Descendants | Are child processes contained and killed? | Prevents timeout escape and orphaned workers |
| Reproducibility | Can the exact image/policy/workspace be replayed? | Supports evidence and debugging |
| Developer friction | Does it work on this host and across platforms? | Determines adoption and fallback risk |
| Observability | Can worker, provider, policy, and cleanup state be inspected? | Enables trustworthy progress and incident response |

A worktree scores well on ownership and reproducibility but poorly on host isolation. A VM scores well on host isolation but costs more. A container scores well on compatibility but shares the kernel. A host broker is therefore more important than any single provider.

### Option assessment

**Temporary directory and Git worktree:** Use for every disposable run and parallel write owner. Copy or export inputs and artifacts instead of mounting broad host paths. A worktree must not be described as a sandbox; linked worktrees share repository refs/config/objects and do not protect credentials, sockets, processes, or external services.

**Bubblewrap plus Landlock:** Best lean Linux composition for a carefully bounded command. Bubblewrap can construct an empty mount namespace, user/PID/IPC/network/UTS namespaces, read-only mounts, tmpfs, and seccomp. Landlock can add irreversible path and port restrictions inherited by descendants. Neither supplies a complete policy by itself. Landlock ABI detection and a policy test are mandatory; a missing capability must fail closed for hostile workloads.

**NsJail:** Prefer when a single wrapper must express cgroups, CPU/memory/PID/file-descriptor/time limits, namespaces, UID/GID mapping, filesystem layout, and Kafel seccomp. Its power increases configuration and audit burden. It is not a reason to grant broad mounts or retained capabilities.

**Rootless Podman:** Prefer when the project wants daemonless OCI execution, per-run containers, explicit `--network` policy, image reproducibility, and container lifecycle commands. Rootless operation still needs subordinate UID/GID configuration, local storage constraints, resource capability checks, and careful handling of `pasta`; no host socket or broad bind mount should be exposed.

**Rootless Docker:** Use where Docker/Compose/API compatibility or existing host operations dominate. Verify that the selected context is actually rootless; a Docker CLI alone does not prove that the daemon is rootless. Resource enforcement depends on cgroup v2/systemd and rootless networking has compatibility/performance limitations.

**Systemd transient unit:** Strong option on a systemd Linux host where the broker can create transient user units. It gives native cgroup lifecycle/resource controls, dynamic users, capability bounds, private mounts/devices, and journal integration. Portability and user-service permissions are the trade-off.

**gVisor:** Middle ground for higher-risk native code when a VM is too heavy. User-space syscall mediation reduces direct host-kernel exposure, with Prometheus/trace support. It can have syscall, filesystem, network, and performance compatibility issues; retain cgroups, no credentials, copied workspaces, and egress controls.

**Kata Containers:** Use when OCI/containerd compatibility and a guest-kernel boundary are needed. It adds VM isolation but also VMM, KVM, virtio, shared-filesystem, and operational complexity. It is a platform choice, not a local first step.

**Firecracker:** Use for a dedicated hostile-code execution service. KVM, minimal devices, Jailer, seccomp, namespaces, cgroups, snapshots, and explicit host networking produce a strong boundary. The broker must build guest images, copy artifacts, mediate network, manage vsock/API, collect logs/metrics, and handle snapshot identity.

**Cloudflare Sandbox:** Use only as a remote managed execution provider. It gives separate VM-backed sandboxes, quotas, lifecycle APIs, and outbound handlers that can keep credentials outside the sandbox. State is lost on container stop unless persisted externally; latency, quota, data residency, network dependency, and Cloudflare trust are material. It is useful for CI or hostile generated candidates, not a transparent local sandbox.

**Claude Code Sandbox Runtime:** The closest direct reference for the desired developer-agent behavior. Anthropic's open beta runtime uses Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux, mediates network through proxies, and can wrap the whole process including MCP servers/hooks. Its configuration and API are beta; the CSM repo should learn from its policy model rather than depend on it as the only provider.

### Recommended policy matrix

| CSM workload | Recommended provider posture | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| csm-plan static discovery | R0; no target execution | Keep planning read-only and cheap |
| csm-plan R&D | R1 or R2 if code runs; synthetic/copy-only inputs | Temporary sandbox is enough only when no hostile code executes |
| csm-ddd | R0; bounded Git/filesystem surface | Analyzer does not execute target code |
| csm-review static | R0 | Static evidence is safer and reproducible |
| csm-review collection/tests | R2 minimum; R3 for suspicious repos | Existing R1-R3 policy already requires egress/env/time controls |
| csm-build implementation | R2 minimum, R3 for unattended or untrusted repositories | Writes and executes code; worktree alone is insufficient |
| csm-make-tests | R2/R3 | Imports, test tools, mutation, benchmarks, and generated code execute |
| registered autoresearch | Trusted in-process only by explicit contract | Registered source is trusted, but still needs bounded loop policy |
| trusted-local autoresearch | R2 recommended; current child process is not OS-isolated | Snapshot/path checks do not contain native process behavior |
| generated autoresearch | R3/R4 verified provider only | Hostile source and evaluator assets need hard containment |
| publication/artifact sink | Separate host-owned capability | Prevent workers from choosing arbitrary destinations or credentials |

### Shared broker contract

The broker should expose provider-neutral typed records:

```text
SandboxPolicy
  provider, trust class, workspace root, output roots, network, credentials
  capabilities, limits, fail mode, attestation, policy digest

SandboxAttempt
  run id, task id, attempt id, provider version, image/policy digest
  started, ended, status, cleanup, descendant status, violations

SandboxResult
  exit status, bounded stdout/stderr refs, artifact refs, evidence refs
  resource observations, policy violations, redacted provenance
```

Required broker invariants:

- Provider capability detection occurs before execution.
- Metadata is not treated as enforcement; the host verifies the provider.
- Input workspaces are copies or explicitly scoped worktrees, never the main checkout by default.
- Writes are allowlisted and artifact export is explicit.
- Environment variables and credential files are scrubbed by default.
- Network is denied by default; allowlists/proxies are explicit and audited.
- CPU, memory, PIDs, file descriptors, disk/output bytes, wall time, and child processes are bounded.
- Timeout kills the complete process group/cgroup and reports cleanup status.
- Sandbox failure is `blocked` or an explicitly approved downgrade, never silent fallback.
- Provider, policy, workspace, artifacts, and events have stable digests and run identity.

### Progress and observability

Sandbox status belongs in the worker event stream proposed by the previous research, with events such as `sandbox.selected`, `sandbox.started`, `sandbox.denied`, `sandbox.violation`, `sandbox.resource-exhausted`, `sandbox.timeout`, `sandbox.cleanup-completed`, and `sandbox.cleanup-unverified`. The dashboard should show provider, policy digest, network mode, workspace mode, heartbeat, resource usage, violations, and cleanup alongside worker progress.

Do not show “sandboxed” as a green security assertion unless the broker has verified the actual provider controls. Display `requested`, `attested`, `degraded`, `blocked`, and `unverified` separately.

recommendation.content:
Recommend this sequence as an architecture decision, not an implementation plan:

1. Define a provider-neutral sandbox capability contract and host-owned execution broker beneath csm-orchestrate.
2. Use the existing Docker installation only after verifying rootless mode, cgroup/resource behavior, network denial, mount restrictions, and whole-process cleanup. Treat the current `docker` binary as availability evidence, not enforcement evidence.
3. Add a bubblewrap/Landlock provider for narrow Linux read-only and single-command workloads, with runtime ABI/capability detection and policy tests.
4. Add a hardened container provider for build, review execution, make-tests, and trusted-local autoresearch.
5. Add gVisor/Kata or Firecracker only when threat-model evidence justifies the operational cost. Use Cloudflare Sandbox for remote managed execution, CI, or hostile workloads when data residency and service dependency are acceptable.
6. Make all provider failures fail closed for generated autoresearch and any workload whose policy requires the missing control.
7. Keep worktree management separate from sandbox management. Worktree cleanup, merge, artifact export, and repository acceptance remain skill-owned concerns.
8. Test the broker adversarially before enabling dynamic workers: credential reads, host path traversal, symlinks, sockets, Docker/Podman sockets, `/proc`, DNS/IPv6, redirects, process storms, fork bombs, memory/output exhaustion, stale descendants, timeout cleanup, duplicate artifacts, and sandbox-unavailable behavior.
9. Reuse existing durable JSON, JSONL, schema registry, artifact resolver, approvals, ledgers, cursors, and receipts rather than creating a parallel persistence system.

Decision rule: choose rootless containers for ordinary local execution, bubblewrap plus Landlock for minimal Linux paths, and VM-backed isolation for hostile/high-value work. Do not choose a provider based on startup speed or marketing alone.

unverifiedClaims.content:
Decision-blocking: the repository has no demonstrated general execution broker for build, review, make-tests, DDD, or autoresearch. Current policy and tests do not prove host-level containment.

Decision-blocking: rootless status, cgroup v2 availability, user namespaces, Landlock ABI, seccomp filters, Docker daemon configuration, and network topology were not fully probed; the host command check found Docker and tmux, but not Podman, bubblewrap, Firejail, or NsJail.

Material risk: rootless Docker/Podman still share the host kernel and can damage host-readable files through mounts or ambient credentials.

Material risk: bubblewrap plus Landlock is not a complete policy and depends on correct mount, descriptor, capability, seccomp, ABI, and network configuration.

Material risk: Firecracker, gVisor, Kata, systemd, Cloudflare Sandbox, and Anthropic Sandbox Runtime have provider-specific compatibility, lifecycle, logging, licensing, version, and operational constraints.

Material risk: Cloudflare Sandbox is remote service infrastructure. Its documented VM isolation, quotas, ephemeral state, and outbound handlers do not remove application authentication, authorization, input-validation, or data-residency responsibilities.

Material risk: “R0” through “R4” in this finding are proposed CSM policy labels, not industry assurance levels.

Material risk: no cited source proves any specific configuration is breakout-proof, secure against kernel/VMM vulnerabilities, or resistant to denial of service under every workload.

Unverifiable: the recommended provider mix will improve productivity, latency, cost, correctness, or user trust without local benchmarks and adversarial tests.

references.content: References are encoded in the top-level `references` array. Official kernel, runtime, vendor, and project documentation is distinguished from local repository evidence and architectural inference. All sources were retrieved or inspected on 2026-08-27.

processAppendix.content:
Triage: DEEP, hybrid. The question affects execution safety for multiple CSM skills and requires current primary sandbox evidence plus local trust-boundary analysis.

Research tracks: (1) Linux user-space sandboxes and host controls; (2) containers, gVisor, Kata, Firecracker, and Cloudflare Sandbox; (3) agent/code-execution security and primary articles; (4) local CSM workload and enforcement mapping; (5) worktrees, temp directories, Claude Code sandbox references, and provider combinations. Five independent read-only researchers returned evidence.

Prior findings consumed: the prior dynamic-workflow and OSS-expansion research notes were read as local evidence. Their worker-runtime, event/snapshot, capability-broker, replay, and skill-boundary conclusions are incorporated but not treated as sandbox proof.

Synthesis: separated workspace isolation, OS isolation, kernel/VMM isolation, network/credential mediation, resource containment, replay, and observability. Compared options by threat model, compatibility, overhead, lifecycle, persistence, and developer friction.

Challenge: the independent challenger downgraded universal “best” claims, mandatory rung assignments, absolute egress wording, and existing-enforcement implications; corrected Cloudflare scope to managed VM-backed sandbox documentation; and required explicit provider-attestation and local host caveats.

Judge pass: the first judge could not score citation/completeness because the artifact did not yet exist. Its required corrections were applied before final synthesis: direct primary references, Cloudflare lifecycle/scope, capability versus enforcement, no-silent-fallback policy, host facts, provider trade-offs, and existing repository gaps.

Verification: this artifact is the sole intended new persistent write for this run; all eight fixed sections are present; citations resolve; journal sequences are contiguous; no credentials or private data are included. The current worktree already contained concurrent untracked `.agents` process artifacts at intake; they were not modified. No code, dependency, sandbox provider, container, or external service was executed or installed by this research run.

citations.quote: Linked worktrees share repository metadata while having separate working files and per-worktree files.
A session temp directory is a writable execution path, so sandboxed and unsandboxed commands resolve different temporary directories.

citations.quote: The Mandatory R&D Safety Gate requires disposable isolation, redirected state, no live credentials, and protected-state verification.

claims.statement: Namespaces, no_new_privs, capabilities, seccomp, Landlock, cgroups, and egress policy are complementary controls rather than individually complete sandbox boundaries.

citations.quote: System call filtering isn't a sandbox.
Landlock is a stackable LSM and applications should check the supported ABI; some filesystem actions remain unrestricted.
cgroups distribute system resources along a hierarchy in a controlled and configurable manner.
Firecracker does not perform network traffic filtering; guest egress should be filtered at host level.

claims.statement: Bubblewrap is a strong lean Linux command-launch primitive, but not universally best and not a complete ready-made sandbox.

citations.quote: Bubblewrap uses user namespaces, creates a new mount namespace, and can add PID/network/UTS/seccomp controls; it is not a complete sandbox with a specific security policy.

claims.statement: Rootless Podman and rootless Docker provide useful containerized execution with different daemon, ecosystem, networking, resource, and host-configuration trade-offs; ordinary containers share the host kernel.

citations.quote: Podman is daemonless and most commands can run as a regular user; rootless mode requires user namespace configuration.
Rootless mode runs the Docker daemon and containers without root inside a user namespace.
Docker uses namespaces and control groups, but capabilities and mounts can provide incomplete isolation.

claims.statement: gVisor, Kata, and Firecracker offer stronger isolation models than ordinary containers with increasing compatibility and operational cost; Cloudflare Sandbox is a remote managed VM-backed isolated-container option with ephemeral lifecycle and outbound controls.

citations.quote: No system call is passed through directly to the host.
Kata provides stronger workload isolation using hardware virtualization as a second layer of defense.
Each Firecracker process encapsulates one microVM and uses KVM plus Jailer, seccomp, cgroups, and namespaces.
Each sandbox runs in a separate VM with filesystem, process, network, and resource isolation.
When a container stops, files, processes, shell state, and interpreter contexts are lost.
